1:
The new speech opens in a changed register. Ellicott hears Eliphaz reply in a far more exaggerated and offensive tone than he has yet adopted, and finds the ground of the whole in a single assertion: the judgment of God cannot be other than disinterested, so that if he rewards or punishes there can be nothing personal in it. Gill accounts for the turn by the speaker's place in the debate. Eliphaz was the first to enter the discussion, and so gives the lead in every course of disputation; but here, angry at Job's arguments and instances, he betakes himself to calumny and reproach and to drawing invidious consequences rather than to solid reasons for conviction.

Gregory the Great asks why a man in that position should state what nobody disputes. Those who are opposed to the words of truth and get the worst in making out a case, he says, often repeat even what is well known, lest by holding their tongue they should seem defeated; and Eliphaz, pressed closely by the sayings of blessed Job, utters things which no one but is aware of. Behind the commonplace he still finds a true distinction, that it is by participation, and not by comparison, with God that we become imbued with wisdom, so that set beside his our knowledge is ignorance.

On the proposition itself there is no division. Gill states it without qualification: there is not anything a man can do by which God can be profited. The goodness of good men extends not to the Lord, since it came from him and was his own previously; having done all that was commanded, they are bid to call themselves unprofitable servants. Henry arrives by way of debt. If God were indebted to us there might be some colour for saying he deals unfairly in afflicting us, so let whoever claims to have made God his debtor prove the debt (Romans 11:35). Clarke turns it on the sufferer: God does not afflict him because he has deprived God of any excellency, and has no interest in his conduct.

The line's other half is allowed its own force. Ellicott takes the clause about the wise man as probably an independent statement rather than a continuation of the question, and Henry builds on that reading: wisdom is profitable to direct (Ecclesiastes 10:10), godliness profitable to all things (1 Timothy 4:8), the wise man wise for himself (Proverbs 9:12). What cannot pass the other way he puts in two figures: the light of a candle is no profit to the sun, nor the drop of the bucket to the ocean. God needs neither us nor our services; we are undone for ever without him, and he is happy for ever without us, which magnifies his condescension in accepting what profits him nothing. Gregory had drawn the same conclusion from the Psalmist, that in all we do well we are doing good to ourselves and not to God, who needs not our goods (Psalm 16:2).

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the verb for being profitable here belongs to this book alone, tracing its sense from the causative form Eliphaz used a few lines earlier (Job 21:21): the root means to rest or dwell, then to dwell beside one another and grow accustomed to one another, and from that to assist and to be profitable. Wesley reduces the thrust to its accusation, asking why Job should insist so much upon his own righteousness as if he obliged God by it. Two of them part from him there. Gill calls the doctrine a very great truth misapplied through a wrong construction of Job's words and meaning, and Henry that it is unjustly applied to Job though in itself very true and good, the innuendo drawn from his complaints being a strained one.
3:
The question about pleasure is answered by distinguishing two senses of the word. Gill grants the first: the Lord does take pleasure in his people, not as sinners but as righteous, as they are considered such in Christ, with his Son's righteousness imputed to them; he is pleased with the new man formed after his image, with the graces of his Spirit, and with their prayers and ready obedience. But none of this gives him any new pleasure or adds to the complacency of his mind, and he would have had as much delight within himself had there never been a holy angel in heaven. Henry puts the same two-sidedness more compactly: God has expressed himself well pleased with the righteous and his delight is in them and in their prayers, while all of it adds nothing to the infinite satisfaction which the Eternal Mind has in itself, and he can enjoy himself without us, though we could have little enjoyment of ourselves without our friends. Wesley narrows the term to the sense Eliphaz needs, a pleasure such as God requires for his own ease and contentment, and Clarke settles it on the divine perfections, infinite, and so neither gaining nor losing by the wickedness or righteousness of men.

The second question turns on motive. Gill explains the human analogy it denies: kings and civil magistrates chastise offenders not only to do justice but sometimes through fear of them, lest if spared or connived at they should be hurtful to the state and overturn it. Sin strikes at God's being and government, yet he stands in no danger of being ruined or dethroned, or of having his government taken out of his hands, and so does not chastise men on that account. Clarke and Wesley each put it as a question with its own answer: is it because he is afraid Job will do him some injury that he has stripped him of power and wealth, and does he punish lest, left alone, Job should grow too great and powerful for him? Surely not; as his righteousness cannot profit God, so his wickedness can do God no hurt.

Henry supplies the political figure and then the history. Princes have sometimes thought it a piece of policy to curb the growing greatness of a subject lest he become formidable, and God is here denied that policy: he does not take a man down from his prosperity for fear he should grow too great, nor enter into judgment with men in the sense of picking a quarrel and seeking occasion against them lest they eclipse his honour. The oldest form of the slander is Satan's to our first parents, that the tree of knowledge was forbidden them lest they should be as gods and so become rivals with him, which Henry calls a base insinuation. Then the instances: Pharaoh oppressed Israel because he feared them, and it was for fear that Herod slew the children of Bethlehem and that the Jews persecuted Christ and his apostles. God does not, as they did, pervert justice for fear of any; he rebukes the good because he loves them, and he never rebukes the great because he fears them.

A second rendering of the clause changes the question entirely. Gill notes that it may be read for thy fear, meaning thy fear of God, thy piety, or as Broughton has it, for thy religion; on that reading Eliphaz is asking whether God chastises a man on account of his godliness, which is close to what Job had often argued, that good men who truly fear God are afflicted by him, so his own sufferings were no objection to his character. Ellicott keeps the first sense but sharpens its edge, taking the line to mean that God stands in awe of Job and asking whether he will therefore justify his dealings with him.
5:
Henry marks this line as the point where the accusation stops being general. Eliphaz and his companions had condemned Job as a wicked man and a hypocrite, but none of them had descended to particulars or drawn up any articles of impeachment until now, when he positively and expressly charges him with many high crimes and misdemeanours. Henry even supplies the reasoning: they had been too long beating about the bush, too tender of Job and afraid of grieving him, which had only confirmed him in his self-justification; condemning him by parables had not prevailed with him to condemn himself, so it was high time to deal plainly and tell him he was the man, the tyrant, the oppressor, the atheist they had been speaking of all this while.

The question answers itself, and Henry reconstructs the inference: certainly the wickedness is great, or else the troubles would not be so great, and Job's own conscience is appealed to as witness. On the second half he pauses over the word. Strictly taken nothing is infinite but God, so what Eliphaz means is that the sins were more than could be counted and more heinous than could be conceived; and Henry allows the usage a defence, since sin committed against Infinite Majesty has in it a kind of infinite malignity. Clarke reads the phrase as duration rather than number, the sins being not only many but great, with no end to Job's continuance in them. Wesley compresses the argument into its arithmetic: the calamities are procured by the sins and proportionable to them. Ellicott refuses the premise outright, calling it mere conjecture and surmise arising from a false assumption, that a just God can punish only the wicked and that therefore those whom he punishes must be wicked.

Gill grants the general doctrine and then shows how little it proves. The wickedness of every man's heart is great, being desperately wicked and full of sin, and out of it comes forth everything that is bad. Degrees are real: sins against God and the first table of the law are greater than those against men and the second, and some are like crimson and scarlet, beams in the eye, while others are comparatively as motes. Yet all are great as committed against God and as breaches of his law, and they appear so most of all to sensible sinners, to whom sin is made exceeding sinful, who own themselves the chief of sinners and ask pardon on that very ground.

Henry turns the occasion into two lessons, and the first is anger at those who censure their brethren unjustly. For aught he can tell, Eliphaz in accusing Job falsely was guilty of as great a sin and as great a wrong as the Sabeans and Chaldeans who robbed him, a man's good name being more precious and valuable than his wealth. It is against all the laws of justice, charity and friendship either to raise or to receive calumnies and evil surmises concerning others, and more base still if those so vexed are already in distress. Eliphaz could produce no instance of guilt under any of the heads that follow, yet seems resolved to calumniate boldly and throw on all the reproach he can, not doubting that some would cleave to him.

The second lesson is pity. Innocency itself is no security against a false and foul tongue: Job, whom God himself praised as the best man in the world, is here represented by one of his own friends, and that friend a wise and good man, as one of the greatest villains in nature. Henry draws from this that we should not think it strange if at any time we are so blackened, but learn to pass by evil report as well as good, and commit our cause, as Job committed his, to him that judgeth righteously.
6:
The first count is a pledge taken for nothing, and Gill will not read the word strictly. It can hardly mean that nothing was lent, but that the sum was trifling and comparatively nothing, or else borrowed for so short a time that no security was needed; and to exact one anyway was unkind, especially from a brother, whether a brother in nature or in religion, a near kinsman, a friend or a neighbour. He records a second rendering that makes it far worse: thou hast taken thy brothers for a pledge, their persons standing as security, to be sold so the debt might be paid, or held as bondmen until it was. Henry takes both readings together. For an inconsiderable debt Job is supposed to have demanded and carried away by violence a pawn of great value, and that from a brother whose honesty and sufficiency he could not but know; and on the rendering Henry credits to the LXX, to have imprisoned and enslaved men because they had nothing to pay.

The stripping is explained as the same act seen from the debtor's side. Wesley glosses it as taking their garment for a pledge, or robbing them of their rights, all other injuries being comprehended under that one. Clarke makes it a settled habit rather than an incident, Job having been vexatious in all his doings and having exacted where nothing was due, so that through him the poor could not procure their necessary clothing. Henry adds the detail that gives the charge its force: the very clothes of insolvent tenants and debtors were taken, so that they were stripped naked and left so, which the law of Moses expressly forbade.

The charge then moves from what was taken to what was refused. Gill fills in the setting: a weary traveller in those hot countries found cold water very refreshing, and in desert places it was not to be had anywhere in common, the wells and fountains belonging to rich men and kept for their own use, so that obtaining water of them was a real favour. Yet a cup of cold water is among the least favours one can do a poor man, and to deny it to him in distress was inhuman, and as far as possible from Job's character. Clarke confirms the custom, furnishing thirsty travellers with water being esteemed a great virtue in the East, especially in the deserts where scarcely a stream was to be found and wells were very rare; some of the Indian devotees, he adds, stand on the public roads with a skin of water for travellers parched with thirst. Henry presses the cheapness of what was withheld, a cup of cold water that would have cost nothing, asked for by a man ready to perish for want of it, and reads the bread clause as the stronger of the two: not merely failing to give, but forbidding the giving, which is withholding good from those to whom it is really due (Proverbs 3:27).

What the charges rest on is the question none of them will leave alone. Wesley has Eliphaz speaking by way of strong presumption, reasoning from the unusual calamities that Job must be guilty of all or some of these crimes. Gill sets out the fork: if these are only conjectures drawn from the afflictions, they are contrary to the charity that thinks no ill and hopes the best; if they are positive assertions of matters of fact, they are worse. Henry calls it all utterly false on the evidence of Job's own account of his conduct (Job 29:12) and of the character God gave him at the outset. Ellicott makes the same judgement about the accuser rather than the accusation, taking these specific charges, false as they were, as a measure of the depth to which Eliphaz had sunk.
8:
The phrase behind "the mighty man" is read as a title. Clarke gives it literally as the man of arm, finger and hand and arm being alike emblems of power, meaning not merely the strong man but the man of influence, of rapine and plunder; and the honourable man is literally the man whose face is accepted. From the pair he draws a double standard: an enemy to the poor and needy, a flatterer of the rich and great. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both point the title at Job himself. Ellicott mentions, and thinks hardly probable, a proposal that the whole run of charges is God's own speech in judgment on Job. Keil and Delitzsch fill out the portrait: he acquired territory far and wide by bringing down the rightful possessors through open violence or by cunning and unfeeling practices, undeterred by any threat of a curse, looking on the land as his and determined that his it must become; and as his possessions grew so did his authority, until he filled the place out alone, like a stout fellow who takes away the room of all others. The address is suspended, they say, to describe the man as he was and is, his dealings regulated by an all-absorbing love of self.

Read the other way, the mighty man is somebody Job indulged. Gill offers both: either he held a large portion of the earth that Job, being the weaker, could not hinder him from enjoying, or else Job gave him more than of right belonged to him, since whenever a cause came before him between a rich man and a poorer one over a piece of land he always gave it to the rich. Wesley allows either, a possession held peaceably by Job's sentence or by his permission, whether the man had right to it or no. Henry makes it a matter of the courts: the mighty man was never questioned for any crime, and whether he brought an unjust action or had a just one brought against him he was sure to carry his cause; the poor were not fed at Job's door while the rich were feasted at his table, against Christ's rule for hospitality (Luke 14:12) and Solomon's word that he who gives to the rich shall come to poverty.

With the widows the charge moves from favouritism to dismissal, and Gill canvasses three places for it. They may have been sent empty out of their own houses, which Job is supposed to have spoiled and cleared of everything, as the Scribes and Pharisees did in Christ's time; or out of his house, where they came for charity and left as they arrived, bidden to depart without food or clothing; or out of his court, where they sought deliverance from their oppressors and were dismissed without justice. Henry takes the harshest of these. Widows who troubled nobody while their husbands lived, and were now forced to seek relief, went from his doors empty and with a sad heart; those who came for justice were sent away unheard; and some who came full were squeezed and sent away empty.

The last clause is passive, and Henry will not let that pass. Eliphaz does not say that Job broke the arms of the fatherless, but means it to be understood so, and his inference is that where such people are broken and those with power do not relieve them, the powerful are chargeable with it: they were broken by those under Job, who connived at it, and the guilt comes back to him. Wesley glosses the arms as their supports and rights. Clarke takes the figure to cover everything they had, whatever strength or power or property, and ends sharpest of all, that Job was hard-hearted and cruel and enriched himself with the spoils of the poor and the defenceless.
10:
The word "therefore" carries the argument, and Henry states the syllogism: men guilty of such practices bring themselves into just such a condition as Job is now in, therefore Job has been guilty. Clarke makes it a rule of exchange: as Job dealt with others, so God in his retributive providence has dealt with him; as he spoiled, so is he spoiled. Gill is careful about which snares are meant: not what occasions sin and draws a man into it, such as inward corruptions, the temptations of Satan and the things of this world, but punishments, the calamities that beset Job on every side until no escape was left. He names them: the cattle driven off, the fire from heaven on the sheep, the wind that brought down the house his children were in, the boils that covered his body.

Clarke supplies a figure. There is an allusion, he thinks, to the hunting of the elephant, driven into an enclosure in the woods and passed from strait to strait until it reaches a point from which it cannot get out, its consternation great and its roaring terrible; so God has hunted Job down as men hunt those dangerous beasts. Henry describes the same without the figure: providence crosses such men so that whichever way they step or look they find themselves in distress, and others are as hard upon them as they had been upon the poor. On the sudden fear he looks inward: consciences terrify and accuse, no sin makes a louder cry there than unmercifulness, and though Job will not own it, guilt of that kind creates the terror. Zophar had insinuated as much earlier.

The darkness is read at two levels. Gill allows a judicial blindness and stupidity of mind, which would have to be Job's case if he could not see the hand of God upon him or the snares about him, but prefers the darkness of affliction. Dispensations of providence are sometimes so dark that a man cannot see the cause of them, which was Job's own complaint when he asked why God contended with him; he can see no light of comfort, being deprived of the light of God's countenance as well as sitting in the outward darkness of adversity, and no end to it and no way out. Henry puts it as bewilderment, men at their wits' end and so amazed they do not know what to do, standing in a mist, in dark waters, in the thick clouds of the sky; and he warns that those who have not shown mercy may justly be denied the comfortable hope of finding it, after which nothing is left to expect but snares and darkness and continual fear. Wesley takes the waters as the usual figure for sore afflictions, and the verse as a choice between fear of further evils and the gross darkness of present misery.

Clarke finds the line's connection with what precedes obscure and suspects the text. A letter has been lost, he thinks, and the word rendered "or" was originally the word for light, which is certainly how the copy used by the Septuagint read it, since they translate that Job's light is changed into darkness, his prosperity into adversity. Houbigant corrects differently, so that the line reads darkness, not light, shalt thou behold; Good makes it a choice between being enveloped in deep darkness and being overwhelmed by a flood. Since the versions all differ and the manuscripts give no help, he settles for a plain sense: Job is so encompassed with darkness that he cannot see his way, and so falls into the snares laid for him. Keil and Delitzsch reject the construction that makes the clause merely incidental, on the affirmative rendering and the interrogative alike, and put it as a direct question: does Job not perceive the darkness and the overflow of waters that covers him?
12:
The premise is granted before it is turned. Gill expounds it: heaven takes its name from its height, and the heaven of heavens, higher than the rest, is the habitation of angels and glorified saints, where God's throne is. He adds that God is not confined there, since the heaven of heavens cannot contain him and he is everywhere; being the principal seat of his majesty, heaven has become one of his names. Henry draws three uses from it: a man cannot be profitable to God, it is folly to contend with him, and he should be addressed with great reverence. Wesley makes the height a vantage point, a high tower from which God looks down to govern and recompense all men's actions.

The inference is imputed rather than quoted. Gill is explicit that Job never said it with his lips, and that Eliphaz only supposed such reasoning in his mind, an invidious consequence drawn from what Job had said about the afflictions of the godly and the prosperity of the wicked, and read as a denial of providence. Henry names the manoeuvre: holding the truth in unrighteousness, turning religion's own artillery upon itself. Bad men, he says, expel the fear of God from their hearts by banishing his eye out of the world, and care nothing what they do once persuaded that God does not know. Keil and Delitzsch supply its pedigree. Because Job has denied that prosperity and adversity are distributed by a law recompensing like for like, Eliphaz fastens on him the unbelief the Psalms often mention, which refuses the God of heaven a knowledge of earthly things, as Epicurus refused it to gods leading a blessed life in the spaces between the worlds.

Clarke objects to the method. Eliphaz attributes infidel and blasphemous sentiments to a man who never held them, as if Job had allowed there was a God but held him so exalted above the stars, with such thick cloud between, that he could see neither the earth nor its inhabitants. Clarke's image for the tactic is memorable: dress a man in a bear's skin and he may be hunted and worried by his own dogs. Job's friends attribute falsities to him, then dilate upon them and draw inferences injurious to his character, as polemic writers in theology and politics often do. Henry describes the same charge without the protest, as atheism and gross impiety thought to lie beneath the injustice, since he that did not fear God did not regard man; Eliphaz wants Job believed an Epicurean, owning the being of God while denying his providence.

Two forms of the denial are distinguished, and both answered. The first makes the clouds an obstruction, and Gill has Job reasoning as atheistical persons do, who take God for such a one as themselves and conclude that because thick clouds hide the stars from human sight they must hide men's actions from God's, whereas nothing stands between God and man. Henry denies the premise: this would require God to have eyes of flesh, whereas the interposing firmament is to him transparent crystal, and distance of place no more a difficulty to him who fills immensity than distance of time to him who is eternal. The second form puts the earth beneath notice. Clarke states it as Eliphaz means it, that God confines himself to those regions and cares nothing for earth's inhabitants, and Wesley that his delight is in heaven while he will not burden himself with the care of earth, an opinion many Heathen philosophers held and fancied was Job's too. Henry calls that absurdity as well as impiety, since it makes government a disparagement to the supreme governor; and if the sun, a creature and inanimate, can light every part of this earth from that height and through thick cloud, the question cannot fairly be raised about the Creator (Psalm 19:6).
15:
Whether the question is about the past or the present is itself disputed. Ellicott re-renders it so that it asks not whether Job has observed the old way but whether he keeps it, and whether he holds the tenets of the men who trod it. Clarke reads it likewise, as one more accusation, that Job walks where the wicked of old walked, and finds an evident allusion to the Flood which the next verse makes explicit. Wesley confines himself to the phrase, glossing it as the way of antiquity, of men living in ancient times, and of their end or success.

Gill identifies the travellers. It is the evil road men have walked ever since the apostasy from God, the course of Cain and his descendants, who were of the wicked one; and since Broughton renders the phrase as the way of the old world, Gill fills in that world's character. The imagination of the thoughts of their hearts was evil continually; they filled the earth with rapine and violence; all flesh corrupted its way with every kind of impurity, and they indulged themselves in their sensual lusts and pleasures, until the Apostle Peter could call them simply the world of the ungodly. The phrase Eliphaz uses means men of wickedness, men who gave themselves up to it and were immersed in it, who trod the tracks of sin until they were beaten smooth, treading them continually, their whole life one unbroken habit of iniquity in which they obstinately persisted and proceeded from evil to evil.

Henry explains why the appeal to history comes here. Having tried to convict Job by setting his sins, as he thought, in order before him, Eliphaz now tries to awaken him to a sense of his danger by setting his case beside that of the sinners of the old world: his condition is bad now, but unless he repents it will be worse, as theirs was who were overflown with a flood, and as was that remnant whom the fire consumed, the men of Sodom being, next to a whole world, no more than a remnant. Henry notes that the two judgments are more than once set side by side as a warning to a careless world, by our Saviour (Luke 17:26) and by the apostle (2 Peter 2:5).

He also suspects a particular target in the choice of examples. Job had argued from the prosperity of the wicked, and the reply is that one may find here and there a single instance of a wicked man ending his days in peace, but that this is nothing against the drowning of the whole world and the burning of Sodom, destructions by wholesale in which Eliphaz means Job to see, as in a glass, his own face. Yet Henry takes the text itself as sound however it is being used. There is an old way which wicked men have trodden; religion had but newly entered the world when sin immediately followed it; and though the track is old and broad and well worn, it is dangerous and ends in destruction, so that marking it is worth doing precisely in order never to dare set foot on it.
16:
The phrase "cut down out of time" bears three senses. Gill allows all three: sent out of time into eternity, since time is no more with men once death seizes them; or before time, short of the term nature would have allowed, which matters here, since if these are the men of the old world many swept off by the deluge might otherwise have lived for centuries; or without time, suddenly and unawares, for though they had notice of the flood they did not regard it but lived secure until it came without further warning. His figures are the axe laid to the root of a tree, to which men in power and flourishing circumstances are sometimes compared, and the scythe, which grass cannot resist. Ellicott prefers snatched away before their time, and draws a consequence nobody else mentions: the allusion to the Flood, if that is what it is, bears on the age of that record, since the book itself can hardly fail to be very old.

What was overflown is read either as ground or as principle. Henry takes the foundation to be the earth on which these men built themselves and all their hopes, overflown by the flood brought upon the world of the ungodly; and he adds that those who build on sand have chosen ground that will be overflown when the rains descend and the floods come, so that the building must fall and they perish in its ruins (Matthew 7:27). Ellicott offers a different construction, that a stream was poured out upon their foundation, or that it became like a flowing stream, which he takes to mean their principles are infectious and bear all before them.

The words in the next line are Job's own, and they all notice it. Wesley puts it squarely: Eliphaz repeats what Job had said, but to a contrary purpose, Job alleging it to show that such men prospered notwithstanding their wickedness and Eliphaz producing it to show they were cut off for it. Gill fills in what the demand amounts to: a refusal to be admonished of sin, exhorted to repentance, instructed in duty, or to be under God's rule at all. Ellicott notes the habit: here again Eliphaz fathers on Job the thoughts he had ascribed to the wicked. Henry has Eliphaz granting the quotation and turning it: those others may have said it and prospered, but these found to their cost what it was to set God at defiance, having abandoned religion, shunned his word and silenced conscience, his deputy.

The closing question is read three ways by Henry. It may mark the justice of the punishment: men who said Depart left the Almighty nothing to do but cut them off, and those who will not submit to a golden sceptre must expect to be broken with an iron rod. It may mark the injustice of the sin: what has the Almighty done against them, what iniquity have they found in him, wherein has he wearied them? Or it may give their own reasoning, that God has done nothing to oblige them and can do nothing in wrath to make them miserable or in favour to make them happy. Henry refutes all of it from one word, the title Almighty: if he is that, what can he not do? Men who neither dread God's wrath nor desire his favour, he adds, will naturally cast off religion. Clarke turns the line into reported speech in the mouths of the unrighteous in the days of Noah, who had abundance of every temporal good and answered Noah's preaching of the terrors of the Lord with a defiance, that the Almighty might do his worst. He adds that for "to them" the Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic evidently read "to us", which quotes the saying directly where the other narrates it, the meaning being the same.
18:
The bounty counts as an aggravation. Gill takes the good things to be temporal ones, good in themselves and in their effects when rightly used, and of which the wicked have their full share: barns filled with corn and wheat, houses with gold and silver and rich furniture. All of it comes from God, the earth being full of his goodness, which shows that they hold it on no merit of their own but by the sovereign pleasure of God, and that his benefits aggravate their wickedness. Henry makes the point from the two examples: the old world and Sodom alike had great plenty of the delights of sense, so that they had no reason to ask what the Almighty could do for them when they lived on his bounty, nor to bid him depart who had been so kind. Many, he adds, have their houses full of goods and their hearts empty of grace, and are thereby marked for ruin.

The repudiation that follows is a quotation, and its tone is read differently. Clarke hears sarcasm. Job had described the wicked who told the Almighty to depart, then added that their counsel was far from him; Eliphaz, having described the impious and ranked Job among them, takes up the same words as though to say his own mind is not contaminated by their creed. Ellicott makes it the climax, the irony reaching its height in the adoption of the very formula of repudiation Job had used. Wesley has him repeat the words not without reflection: Job said this against his own principle that God carries himself indifferently towards good and bad, whereas one who has observed God's terrible judgments has far more reason to abhor their counsels. Henry alone takes it straight: Job had said it and Eliphaz will not be behind him, and if the two cannot agree in their principles concerning God they agree in renouncing the principles of men who live without God.

Henry turns that agreement into a rule: men who differ in some matters of religion ought still to appear unanimously against atheism and irreligion, and to see their disputes do not weaken their unanimity in that common cause. On the gladness of the righteous he is careful about its object: not at seeing fellow creatures miserable, nor at any secular turn of their own being served, but at seeing God glorified, his word fulfilled, the power of oppressors broken and the oppressed relieved, sin shamed, and fair warning given to everyone else. The scorn he allows on the same terms, since they will laugh as God laughs, in a holy manner, exposing the folly of sinners and showing how ridiculous their principles are though they call themselves wits.

Gill draws the same distinction and gives three reasons. What the righteous see is not the counsel of the wicked nor their prosperity but their ruin, which is sure, and often visible, such men being made public examples. The misery of a fellow creature could not please them as misery, which would be brutish and inhuman and displeasing to God himself. They are glad partly because they have been kept from the sins that bring such ruin, partly because they are delivered from the men who were distressing them, and chiefly for the glory of the divine perfections. Clarke puts it as submission rather than relief: they see God's judgments on the incorrigibly wicked, know the Judge of all the earth does right, and rejoice in all the dispensations of his providence. Keil and Delitzsch set the verse beside the close of many Psalms, where the same thing is a wish or a hope: the retributive justice of God, however long the wait, becomes at length the more gloriously manifest to the joy of those innocently persecuted; and the mockery is aimed at the ungodly, whose mocking pride comes to that ignominious end.
20:
Who is speaking in this line is the first question. Ellicott takes it for the words of the righteous and the innocent, and renders it so: surely they that did rise up against us are cut off, and the remnant of them the fire hath consumed. He thinks the Authorised Version's wording less correct, though on that reading too the words belong to the innocent of the previous verse. Gill canvasses the options and rejects two. It might be made to mean Noah and his family, preserved in the ark with the creatures and with sustenance laid up for them all while everything belonging to the ungodly perished, which he judges too restrictive, or the subtler claim that the human race itself was not cut down in the flood but preserved in that family and restored through it. He prefers to hear Eliphaz and his friends ranking themselves among the righteous and the innocent and rejoicing with them, with a particular eye on Job's case: his estate cut down and himself stripped bare, theirs untouched and in their full possession, the reason assigned being his guilt and their innocence. Others, he adds, also hear the verse as the triumph of the righteous.

Wesley fastens on the pronoun. The speaker should have said their substance and instead says ours, either because he counts himself among good men and means to indicate that he pleads the common cause of all such while Job pleads the cause of the wicked, or because he wishes to acknowledge with thanks some particular preservation granted to himself among the rest. Henry hears the same note and will not let it stand. The sense he gives it is that their substance is not cut down as the old world's was and as Job's is, that they continue to prosper, and that their prospering is a sign of being Heaven's favourites and in the right. The rule that served to condemn Job serves equally to magnify the man applying it: his substance is cut down, therefore he is wicked; ours is not, therefore we are righteous. Henry calls that a deceitful rule to judge by, since no one knows love or hatred from all that is before him, and he puts the proper response in its place. When others are consumed and we are not, we ought to be thankful to God and take it as a warning to prepare for the like calamities, rather than censure them and lift up ourselves.

Clarke reads the two halves as the two great judgments. Those who fear the Lord still continue in health and peace, while those who departed from him are destroyed down to their very remnant, which he identifies: a flood took off the world of the ungodly in the days of Noah, and those who persisted in that same manner of life were consumed by fire in the days of Lot. Wesley reads the clause the same way, the remnant being all that was left undestroyed in the general calamity and the fire being Sodom and Gomorrah. Clarke also records a different construction of the word rendered "our substance", which Good takes to be the same as an Arabic word for a people or a tribe, and translates accordingly: our tribe is not cut off, while even the remnant of these a conflagration consumed. What Clarke will not leave unsaid is the use the two examples are being put to. Eliphaz brings them in to terrify Job into compliance with the exhortation that follows immediately, so that the history is not offered as history but as leverage.
21:
The speech changes character here, and the change is noticed with relief. Gill observes that Eliphaz passes from severe charges to advice and exhortation, and seems in a better temper, the only fault being the false supposition behind it; given a proper object, the discourse would have been excellently said. Henry says he can almost forgive the hard censures for the sake of this counsel, than which nothing could be better said, since Eliphaz thought Job a bad man and yet hoped he would be both pious and prosperous. What he finds strange is that sweet waters and bitter should proceed out of the same mouth almost in the same breath, which he accounts for by remarking that good men, once put into a heat, will sometimes talk themselves into a better temper, sooner than another could talk them into it.

Henry also explains the strategy: the misery of the wicked was set out to frighten Job into repentance, and the happiness of those who repent is now set out to allure him to it, ministers having to try both ways, Mount Sinai by the terrors of the law and Mount Sion by the comforts of the gospel.

The opening imperative is rendered several ways. Some read it as acquiesce in God, which Henry takes to be our duty at all times and especially in affliction, quieting ourselves in all the disposals of divine Providence. He thinks the translators have done well with acquaint thyself with him, since what is asked is that a man cease being the stranger to God he has made himself by casting off the fear of him and restraining prayer; and he spells out what that involves: getting the knowledge of him, fixing the affections on him, joining ourselves to him in a covenant of friendship, and keeping up a constant correspondence in the ways he has appointed. Clarke proposes another sense, that the verb means treasure up, so that the counsel is to procure an interest now with God, since whoever gets the divine favour is at peace with him. Gill draws out what the exhortation presupposes, an estrangedness that is every man's case from the womb, acquaintance beginning at conversion, when God is made known not only as the God of nature but as the God of grace and peace in Christ, and carried on by prayer and attendance on his worship.

On the peace, Henry hears two at once. There is peace with oneself, not fretful or uneasy but quiet and well composed, and peace with God, which means being reconciled and not carrying on this unholy war: Job complains that God is his enemy, and the remedy is for Job to be God's friend. That peace is necessary to any comfortable acquaintance, since two cannot walk together unless they are agreed (Amos 3:3), and it must be made now, while a man is still in the way. One reading turns the imperative into entreaty, acquaint thyself, I pray thee, with him, which Henry finds fitting, since God beseeches us and ministers in Christ's stead pray us to be reconciled. Wesley lists what renewing the acquaintance takes: prayer, repentance, true humiliation under God's hand, compliance with his commands, and diligent care to serve and enjoy him. The promise attached is read generously. Henry takes the good to be what has now departed, all the heart can desire, temporal and spiritual and eternal, with God himself coming into covenant and bringing all good with him; Clarke divides it in two, an interest in the divine favour from which every blessing may be expected, and a peace in the conscience that is unutterable happiness, to be got now, since no one knows what a day may bring. Ellicott offers the alternative that thine increase shall be good, or that what comes is rest from the obstinate questionings Job was disturbed with.
22:
Whether "the law" here means the law of Moses divides them. Gill says not, since it is a question whether that code yet existed or could have reached Job, and he takes the term in its wider sense of any doctrine, any revelation of God's mind and will made to the patriarchs and handed down from one to another, to be taken as coming from the mouth of God and not as the word of man, welcomed with reverence and gladness, and not merely attended to but obeyed. Clarke rejects that with open impatience. Some who wish to place Job before Moses say the Noahic precepts are meant, others the law of nature, and he calls both stuff and vanity. The allusion, he holds, is plainly to the statute given to the children of Israel, called here by way of emphasis the Law, containing his Words, the sayings of God himself, which neither of those alternatives can be, since neither was ever written or registered as the words of God's mouth.

Ellicott weighs both sides and settles nothing. It would be highly interesting, he says, to know whether the Torah is alluded to here. One is naturally disposed to think that since this seems to be the one Gentile book of the Old Testament, where the literature of Israel touches the world at large, it must either be prior to the Law or else written in independence and ignorance of it. The former he judges far more reasonable, the life depicted appearing to be that of patriarchal times before the Law was given. Yet he grants the difficulty on the other side: it is hard to know what "his words" could mean before the Mosaic Revelation, unless the expression witnesses to a consciousness of that inner revelation of the voice of God in the conscience which the holy in all ages have never wanted. Henry assumes as much without arguing it: though we do not know that there was any written word in Job's time, there was a revelation of God's will to be received.

What accepting it amounts to is put as government. Henry has Eliphaz urging that a man at peace with God should submit to his rule, and grounds the demand in a sequence: we have our being and our maintenance from God, from him we hope for our bliss, and from him we must take law. However the intimations of his will reach us, by scripture, ministers, conscience or Providence, we are to keep our eye on him and bow our souls to it; and in just this consists the conversion of a sinner, that he takes his law from God and no longer from the world and the flesh. Wesley puts it as a choice of rule: take the standard for your thoughts and words and whole life not from your own imaginations or passions but from God, from his law written in your own mind and from the instructions of holy men, and do not only hear them with your ears but let them sink into your heart.

The second clause concerns retention. It is not enough to hear the word, Henry says; we must keep it, laying it up as a thing of great value so that it may be safe, and in the heart as a thing of great use, ready when occasion arises, so that we neither lose it wholly nor are at a loss for it in need. He also notices what the appeal does to the argument: Eliphaz, in contest with Job, refers the controversy to the word of God and asks to be determined by it. Keil and Delitzsch render the line in a way that bears on the first dispute, having Job receive teaching from God's mouth and place his utterances in his heart, keeping the wider sense rather than binding it to a written code.
23:
The condition is read as demanding a thorough turn. Wesley says the Hebrew phrase is emphatical and implies a turning from sin to God, so as to love him and cleave to him and devote oneself to his service; Keil and Delitzsch find the same force in the preposition, which is not the construction otherwise usual and so marks a thorough conversion. Henry presses it hardest, following Poole: not merely turning from sin but turning to God and duty, and not merely turning towards the Almighty in some good beginnings but returning home to him, quite to him, by a universal reformation and a firm resolution to cleave to him. Gill reads encouragement in the divine name rather than demand. Returning supposes a departure by sinning, needing repentance and confession; and the name used signifies one who is sufficient, all-sufficient, whose hand is not shortened nor his ear heavy, whose grace suffices to receive backsliders and keep them safe.

What is promised in return is reconstruction. Clarke takes being built up as restoration to the former prosperity, with a household again, not of servants only but of children; Wesley the same, that God will repair the ruins and give more children. Henry divides the rebuilding three ways, the family built up in children, the estate in wealth and the soul in holiness and comfort. Keil and Delitzsch note that the verb carries whichever sense the context requires, sometimes building round about or finishing a building, sometimes building up again, and of persons either increasing prosperity or restoring prosperity in ruins, which is the sense here; and the promise stands hedged with conditions, the second clause being added for embellishment.

The clause about iniquity is part of that second condition, and Henry notes it had been Zophar's advice already. Wickedness is not to dwell in the tent; iniquity is to be put far off, the further the better, not from the heart and hand only but from the house, since a man must restrain sin in those under his charge, family reformation being needful reformation. Wesley allows two senses: a spiritual promise, that sincere repentance brings grace to reform a man and his household; or a temporal one, that he shall put away iniquity in the sense of its punishment, far from all his dwellings and possessions. Ellicott adds only what the counsel presupposes, the imputation of apostasy and iniquity to Job.

On the gold Henry finds three assurances. Eliphaz suspected Job's riches had come by fraud and oppression and been taken away for it; but on returning he should have more than before, not sheep and oxen only, the wealth of farmers, but thousands of gold and silver, the wealth of princes. He should hold it more securely too, by a surer tenure than iniquity got, the word for silver meaning silver of strength, which honestly got wears well. And he should be kept from setting his heart on it, laying up gold not as his portion but as dust and as the stones of the brooks, valuing it so little that he lays it at his feet rather than in his bosom. Ellicott makes that last point the sense of the line itself, reading it as a command to put treasure on a level with the dust and the gold of Ophir among the stones of the brooks, reckoning it of no more worth; and the wealth for which Job was famous among the children of the East is here treated as an accumulation of wrong-doing. Clarke holds the line is not fairly rendered at all, and sets the versions side by side: Montanus fixes a tower upon the dust and finds Ophir's torrents in the rock, the Vulgate gives flint for earth and torrents of gold for flint, which Calmet paraphrases as massive gold where stone served before, and Good makes fountains gush amidst the rocks.
25:
The word rendered "defence" is also the word for gold, and the ambiguity is exploited rather than resolved. Henry points it out: the marginal reading makes God the man's gold, the same term as in the previous verse, but it also signifies a strong-hold, since money is a defence (Ecclesiastes 7:12); worldlings make gold their god, and saints make God their gold. Ellicott prefers treasure outright, rendering it that the Almighty shall be a treasure and precious silver, and notes that the word qualifying silver occurs only three other times, its idea being probably brightness or splendour. Keil and Delitzsch render the two nouns as gold ore in abundance and silver of the brightest lustre. Gill takes both halves at once: the Almighty secures the gold and silver already possessed, so that no Sabeans or Chaldeans can break in and carry it off, and is himself the truest riches, earthly gold being contemptible beside him.

Gill carries the defence into the spiritual register too: preservation from sin and Satan and the world, a wall of fire about a man, his fortress and tower. Henry draws the contrast with what wealth usually does. Riches commonly expose their owners to danger, and Job had owned that in his prosperity he was not in safety; the promise is that his wealth shall no longer lie exposed to spoilers, which Henry thinks may also be the sense of putting iniquity far from the tabernacle, read as a promise that the wrong designed against a man shall never reach him. Those must needs be safe, he concludes, who have Omnipotence for their defence. Clarke reads the surrounding verses as a catalogue of how precious metals are got, gold in dust, gold in hill streams, silver in mines, the phrase for silver meaning silver of giddiness, from mines so deep that looking in makes one dizzy.

Clarke will not let the promise pass as theology. The versions and the critics vary, he says, but the doctrine of Eliphaz is plain: God gives the most earthly good to those he loves best, the rich and the great are his high favourites, and he holds the poor and the distressed for his enemies. On the next line what Eliphaz offers is that Job shall know from his prosperity that God favours him, and be grateful for the bounty. How different, Clarke asks, is the doctrine of the apostles, where peace with God comes by justification through faith, where the Spirit of the Son bears witness that we are children of God, where men glory in tribulation because it works patience and patience hope, and where we love him because he first loved us. Tribulation itself, he ends, was often a mark of God's favour.

On the delight they are warmer. Gill locates it in the perfections of God's nature, the works of his hands, his word and worship, communion with him, and the relation he stands in as their covenant God and Father, conditional on the affections being drawn off earthly riches first. Henry turns the sequence round: the way to have our heart's desire is to make God our heart's delight, and if God gives us himself for our joy he will deny us nothing good for us. He also notes the change implied, since God is at present a terror to Job by his own confession, and it shall become as much a pleasure to think of him as it has been a pain. The lifted countenance he reads as humble holy confidence, such as those have whose hearts do not condemn them: a man whose face is fallen shall blush no more, tremble no more and hang his head no more, but show himself cheerfully to God and expect blessings from him. Wesley says only, look up to him with cheerfulness and confidence; Ellicott notes Zophar had promised the same.
27:
What kind of praying is meant comes out of the verb. Gill takes it in a supplicating, entreating sense, pleading not merit but mercy, and not for a man's own righteousness' sake but for the Lord's and for Christ's; and since the word also means to multiply, prayer is to be made always and without ceasing. He adds that it is addressed to God only, no creature being prayed to, and that it is as much privilege as duty, since a man may come to God as his Father through Christ the Mediator, and to a throne of grace where mercy is found to help in time of need. Clarke glosses the verb more physically: thou shalt open or unbosom thyself, and when the heart prays God hears, so that the man, being blessed, vows fidelity and is enabled to pay his vows. Wesley reports only that the word is multiply, every burden and want and fear being matter to send to heaven for wisdom, strength and comfort.

Henry turns the promise into a figure of correspondence: the exchange, once settled, is kept up, letters interchanged between a man and heaven at set times and as occasion arises. Prayer sends the letters, and God will not find them troublesome though many and long, since the oftener we come to the throne of grace the more welcome. He answers by providence and grace, giving what is asked either in kind or in kindness, and making it plain he has heard by what he does for a man and in him. Praise then replies, which is what paying the vows amounts to, and that fetches in further mercy. The obligation he draws is exact: when God performs what we prayed for we must make conscience of performing what we then promised, or we do not deal honestly; and if we promised nothing else we promised thankfulness, which is enough because it includes everything. Wesley puts it plainly: the blessings obtained are those the vows were made for.

On decreeing a thing Gill is scrupulous: strictly the language belongs to God alone, whose decrees cannot be frustrated, the usual saying being that man appoints and God disappoints. He offers three ways of taking it of a man: as a magistrate, decreeing with such wisdom and equity that the decree stands firm and, though made on earth, is ratified in heaven; or as a private man, so prospered that whatever he lays a scheme to execute is brought about, since committing his ways to the Lord establishes his thoughts; or, as he prefers, as a praying man, which agrees with the line before. Clarke puts it in a clause: whatever a man purposes in God's strength he shall accomplish, and Wesley that his purposes shall not be disappointed but ratified. Keil and Delitzsch render it as devising a plan that is established. Ellicott supplies an instance, Abraham's intercession for Sodom, to which he thinks there is probably an allusion.

Henry reads the same clause as inward satisfaction in outward affairs. A man shall frame his projects with so much wisdom and resignation to God's will that the issue is to his heart's content; he commits his works to the Lord by faith and prayer, his thoughts are established, and he is easy whatever occurs. This the grace of God works in him, though sometimes providence gives the very thing desired, in its own way and time. When an affair succeeds just according to the scheme laid, Henry says the promise has been performed. The light he reads as guidance with prosperity following: Job now complains of darkness round about him, and light shall shine on his ways, God's wisdom his guide and favour his comfort, so that he has a comfortable enjoyment of the present and prospect of what is to come. Wesley compresses it to direction and governance, comfort and success.
29:
The first line sets a man's steadiness against a general collapse. Gill reads the cast down as the wicked brought out of prosperity into adversity, left in low circumstances and great straits; Wesley takes it of everyone round about in a time of general calamity, the lifting up being God's deliverance of the man addressed. Henry fills in the collapse and the answer: men cast down in their affairs and in their spirits, sinking, desponding and ready to despair, while the man who has returned finds something in himself that will not only bear him up but lift him above his troubles. What lifts him is the belief that God will save the humble person, and Henry insists on both halves of the exaltation, in honour and in comfort.

How the line should be construed is less agreed. Clarke calls it a great difficulty, though the sense he thinks tolerably evident, and offers a nearly literal version making the humbling the men's own act: when they shall humble themselves, thou shalt say, there is exaltation, for the down-cast of eye he will save. In that he hears the same sentiment as our Lord's, that he who exalts himself shall be abased and he who humbles himself shall be exalted. Ellicott allows the usual rendering but records a sourer one, on which what the man says when others go down is that pride caused their fall. Keil and Delitzsch reject the construction, referring the verb not to men but to a man's ways, since the word for making low can also mean to go down and, of ways, to lead downwards; the old expositors went astray, they add, for not discerning the exclamative force of the word that follows.

The word "island" is given up by everyone who examines it. Gill asks where there is any such thing as an island of innocent persons, notes that others render it better as the innocent delivering the island, which is true enough since good men are sometimes the means of saving a country by their counsel and above all by their prayers, and observes that the word is really a negative particle meaning not, as the Targum takes it. Clarke reaches the same verdict another way, taking the word for a particle meaning whosoever or any, so that God shall deliver every innocent person, and the innocent be delivered by the pureness of a man's hands, since whoever loves justice does justice. Where the text reads thy hands the Vulgate, Syriac and Arabic read his, and Good takes the word for house; but island must be given up, since it cannot make any consistent sense.

Read as a negative the line says something stranger. Ellicott calls it undoubtedly an error for he shall deliver him that is not innocent, the humble-minded man saving those who could not be saved on their own account, as the ten righteous would have saved Sodom. Henry arrives there by the same reasoning, that the innocent may be supposed not to need deliverance, since it was guilty Sodom that wanted Abraham's intercession, and he draws the rule that a good man is a public good, sinners faring the better for saints whether they know it or not. Keil and Delitzsch suspect a sting, since the not-guiltless may be Job himself in his present condition, a mild periphrasis for the guilty man who has merited his suffering. They notice how the promise turned out: Ellicott calls this last word of Eliphaz a prophecy, because it is exactly how the history closes, and Wesley says that Eliphaz and his two friends, who in this matter were not innocent, were delivered by the pureness of Job's hands. Clarke ends with a verdict on the speech: it began with a tissue of the bitterest charges, continued with the cruellest insinuations, closed with common-place exhortations, and yielded scarcely one important maxim.
